title: Geographic and Temporal Trends in Fake News Consumption During the 2016 US Presidential Election
screen_reason: Behavioural browser-telemetry study (Internet Explorer 11 + Edge, 114 days to election day 2016) of visits to 70 third-party-listed fake news domains. Reports (a) the share of users visiting any fake news domain on an average day — 0.34%, a REACH estimate — and (b) that the top five domains account for 80% of all fake news visitations, a source-level CONCENTRATION estimate.

estimates.country: United States (visits carry ZIP codes; analysis is by US state and FIPS county)
estimates.platform: Desktop web browsing (Internet Explorer 11 and Edge instrumentation)
estimates.date: 18 July 2016 (start of the Republican national convention) to 8 November 2016 (election day); 114 days
estimates.measure_type: % of browser users who visited any monitored fake news domain on an average day during the election campaign
estimates.value_raw: 0.34% of users (i.e., about 1 in every 290 users), average day
estimates.denominator: Users of Internet Explorer 11 and Edge desktop browsers (combined install base of more than 10^8 machines) on an average day between 18 July and 8 November 2016; the exact daily user count is not reported
estimates.definition: Visited at least one of the 70 web domains listed as serving fake news, on that day
estimates.misinfo_def: “Wikipedia defines fake news websites as those which ‘intentionally publish hoaxes and disinformation for purposes other than news satire’.”
estimates.n: Not reported numerically; denominator is the IE11/Edge user base (>10^8 machines installed)
estimates.source_quote: during the election campaign period, only 0.34% of users visited
estimates.page_loc: §4.1 Traffic Sources and Prevalence, p. 2072 — full sentence, broken across line breaks in the text file: 'However, the analysis also reveals that visits to fake news websites were relatively rare—on an average day during the election campaign period, only 0.34% of users visited any of the fake news domains that we monitored (i.e., about 1 in every 290 users).'
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Third-party domain lists only: Wikipedia's 'List of fake news websites' (accessed 22 Dec 2016 and again 25 Jan 2017), Snopes's Field Guide to Fake News Sites and Hoax Purveyors, plus the web domains of the top five fake news stories reported by Silverman (BuzzFeed) — 70 domains in total. No article-level verification and no reliability statistic; the authors explicitly warn that the listed sites carry 'a mix of opinion pieces, and biased fact-based stories that may present events out of context, in addition to articles that are entirely fabricated'.
estimates.moderator_quote: We analyze 114 days of instrumentation data for Internet Explorer and Edge, two desktop web browsers with a combined install base of more than 108 machines. ... The dataset consists of a list of timestamped visits to URLs, together with anonymous user identifiers and ZIP codes. Of interest are visits to 70 fake news web domains as outlined in Section 2.
estimates.notes: WINDOW MATTERS: this is a per-DAY reach (share of users visiting any fake news domain on an average day), not cumulative reach over the 114-day campaign — it is therefore far smaller than a campaign-period reach figure and must not be pooled with cumulative-window reach estimates. The user denominator is never stated numerically (only 'more than 10^8 machines' installed), so no counts are recoverable. Country coded United States because every reported analysis is US-geographic (ZIP codes, states, FIPS counties), but note the paper never explicitly says the 0.34% denominator is restricted to US users while the IE/Edge install base is global — a real ambiguity. topic=politics_elections reflects the election framing and the fact that all five top-traffic domains are political, but the authors deliberately kept non-political fake news domains (pseudoscience, health, celebrity/sports gossip) in the list 'so as to avoid editorializing', so the corpus is not topic-restricted. breadth='' per the schema rule for source-level lists. Desktop IE/Edge only — no mobile, which the authors flag as a major coverage limit.

estimates.notes: R1 satisfied: conc_share_pct = 80 is verbatim; conc_group_pct = 7.1 is 5/70, an exact part/whole from two verbatim counts (the five top domains named in Table 1, out of the 70 monitored domains stated in §3), which R8 permits. CAVEAT for the adjudicator: the paper never says how many of the 70 domains actually received any traffic, so 7.1% is the share of MONITORED domains, not of domains with non-zero visits — the true concentration among active domains is therefore at least this steep. within_misinfo_content=true because the denominator is fake-news visits only (concentration inside the misinformation set), which is intrinsic to the CONCENTRATION construct here. unit='exposure' because the quantity being concentrated is visits; conc_unit='source' carries the group unit. confidence=medium only because conc_group_pct is derived rather than stated.

missed_or_uncertain: (1) '68% of all page visits for which traffic sources could be determined' came from social media, and '99% of social media referrals coming from Facebook', plus the per-domain social-referral shares in Table 1 (endingthefed.com 97.6%, thepoliticalinsider.com 80.0%, infowars.com 10.9%, americannews.com 98.9%, libertywritersnews.com 96.7%). These are referral-SOURCE breakdowns computed inside fake-news traffic — they say where fake news traffic came from, not what share of anything was fake news — so they are not prevalence and no row was created. An adjudicator wanting a 'channel' moderator will find them here. (2) Figures quoted from other work and barred by R8: Allcott & Gentzkow's estimate that 'about 1.2% of the population was exposed to the average fake news article', their X = 7.6 × 10^6 pro-Clinton and Y = 3.0 × 10^7 pro-Trump story shares, the 0.90% Facebook news-feed ad click-through rate, and the 51.7% mobile-exclusive Facebook user figure. (3) Pearson correlations between fake-news visitation and Trump vote share (state r = 0.85, county r = 0.71, Romney r = 0.76, and Table 2's weekly r = 0.84–0.88) are associations, not prevalence. (4) Maximum-visitation-rate distributions (Figure 3) and the four story case histories (Figure 2) are temporal shapes with no denominator. (5) No cumulative (whole-campaign) reach figure is reported — only the average-day figure — so the more commonly pooled 'share of people who saw any fake news during the campaign' cannot be recovered from this paper.

rob.design: Observational browser-telemetry study. Data: 114 days (18 July – 8 November 2016) of instrumentation from Internet Explorer 11 and Edge, combined install base >10^8 machines, collected with user permission to support predictive services; records are timestamped URL visits with anonymous user identifiers and ZIP codes. Exposure definition is purely source-level: 70 domains taken from Wikipedia's fake-news-website list, Snopes's Field Guide, and Silverman's top-five story domains, with no article-level verification and no reliability assessment. Election data from Dave Leip's Atlas of U.S. Presidential Elections. Coverage limits: desktop only, IE/Edge only — no mobile and no other browsers, which the authors flag as a first-order limitation; no user denominators, sampling weights, or demographic adjustment are reported, so the user base is a non-representative convenience trace. The authors also concede that the listed domains mix fabricated stories with opinion and biased-but-factual reporting, and explicitly warn against causal inference from the voting correlations.
